name: Mass gainer powders

card.summary: Calorie-dense carb-and-protein shake powders for lifters who struggle to eat enough; they add calories, and the evidence is about overall energy intake rather than the powder itself.
card.note: Some products have been linked to contamination with undeclared steroids; one case report links a steroid-containing mass gainer to pancreatitis.

quick.overview:
A mass gainer is a powdered supplement mixed into a shake that delivers a large number of calories per serving, usually from carbohydrate, protein and fat. It is aimed at people trying to gain body weight and muscle who find it hard to eat enough food.

According to Grokipedia, typical servings supply 500 to 1,500 calories with a protein-to-carbohydrate ratio of around 1:2 or more [1]. Looksmaxxing forum users disagree about whether they are useful or whole food is preferable [2].
quick.mechanism: The mechanism is a caloric surplus: eating more energy than is used is needed to gain weight, and resistance training directs part of the gain toward muscle. A powder is a convenient, energy-dense way to add calories, often built on whey and maltodextrin [1]. A registered overfeeding-plus-resistance-training trial has examined body composition changes under surplus feeding, but results are not described in the registration [3].
quick.risks: Dietary supplements in the US are regulated as foods and manufacturers confirm product safety themselves [4]. A review of FDA data found muscle-building products among those contaminated with undeclared anabolic steroids [4], and a 2025 case report describes pancreatitis with panniculitis in a patient who took a weight-gain supplement thought to contain anabolic steroids [5]. Users also report digestive complaints and acne in forums [2].

lead: A mass gainer, or weight gainer, is a high-calorie powder supplement designed to help people gain weight and muscle by supplying a large amount of energy, mostly from carbohydrate with moderate protein and some fat, in a drinkable form [1]. For someone trying to build a fuller physique, the appeal is practical: a shake can add several hundred to over a thousand calories without the volume of a full meal, which helps people who find it hard to eat enough to sustain a calorie surplus alongside resistance training [1].

Mass gainers are discussed in bodybuilding and looksmaxxing communities by 'hardgainers' and by people bulking. Some lifters regard them as a convenient way to hit calorie targets; others in the same forums argue that whole foods or plain protein are preferable [2]. Typical products combine whey protein concentrate, a fast-digesting carbohydrate such as maltodextrin, and fats, sometimes with vitamins, minerals and digestive enzymes [1][8].

Evidence specific to mass gainers as a product category is limited. The underlying principle, that weight gain requires a caloric surplus and that resistance training directs the surplus toward muscle, is general nutrition; research on protein supplementation during resistance training and published case reports of harms from adulterated products form the nearest literature [5][6].

chain: Powder supplies a large amount of calories per shake
Easier to reach a calorie surplus
With resistance training, more weight and muscle gained
angle.text: Lifters who struggle to eat enough use mass gainer shakes to add calories in a convenient form during bulking. Combined with resistance training, the surplus is the route to a larger, fuller physique.

paras: Grokipedia describes mass gainers as combining whey protein concentrate, rapidly absorbed carbohydrate such as maltodextrin, and fats such as medium-chain triglyceride oil, sometimes with added vitamins, minerals, amino acids and digestive enzymes; plant-based versions use pea or rice protein and tapioca-based carbohydrate [1]. They differ from whey isolate products, which focus on protein with fewer calories [1]. Example product labels cited there give about 1,250 calories and 50 g of protein for a two-scoop serving [1].

Whey protein is a mixture isolated from the liquid left over from cheese making; the concentrate form keeps lactose, while isolate has fat and lactose removed and is typically over 90 percent protein [7]. Digestible maltodextrin is a glucose polymer that is broken down quickly into glucose and is used in sports drinks and recovery products because it is absorbed rapidly [8]. Its glycemic index is reported as 110, and Wikipedia notes that large amounts can cause rapid blood sugar rises, a concern for people with diabetes or insulin resistance [8].

Grokipedia traces calorie-dense muscle-building products to late 19th-century items such as Bovril and Plasmon, and says homemade high-calorie shakes of milk, eggs and bananas were promoted to bodybuilders in the 1970s and 1980s, with commercial products from firms such as Weider and Optimum Nutrition following; it adds that online retail in the 2000s widened availability and that the 2010s brought clean-label and plant-based versions [1]. These historical claims come from an AI-generated encyclopedia and have not been independently verified here.

Wikipedia's account of bodybuilding supplements notes earlier landmarks: Eugen Sandow promoted dietary control in the 1910s, Irvin P. Johnson popularised egg-based protein powders in the 1950s, and the industry grew rapidly in the 1970s and 1980s [6]. Whey protein concentrate suitable for drinks was developed in New Zealand in 1970 after a request from Coca-Cola, which is part of the dairy-industry origin of the ingredient [7].

In general terms, Grokipedia describes common practice as one or two servings a day, often after training or between meals, alongside resistance training and whole-food meals, with some users starting with smaller servings to limit digestive upset and tracking body weight and composition [1]. Lifters describe them as a way of reaching calorie targets during a bulk, the phase of deliberate surplus eating intended to add muscle [1][2]. Plant-based and lactose-free versions exist for users who avoid dairy [1].

US and Canadian guidelines set the recommended protein intake for a sedentary adult at about 0.8 g per kg of body weight per day, while sports-nutrition recommendations for strength athletes are around 1.4 to 1.8 g per kg per day [10]. A 2018 meta-analysis by Morton and colleagues, as summarised on Wikipedia, found that protein supplementation enhanced strength and muscle size gains during resistance training, with gains plateauing at around 1.6 g per kg per day [6]. Wikipedia's protein article also states that people with a balanced diet do not need protein supplements, and that no conclusive evidence shows high protein intake causes chronic kidney disease, though people with existing kidney disease are advised to reduce protein [10].

In the US, DSHEA (signed 25 October 1994) treats supplements as foods; manufacturers do not need FDA approval before sale, and the FDA generally acts after a problem arises [4][9]. A study of supplements sold from 2007 to 2016 found 776 products with undeclared pharmaceuticals, and muscle-building products were contaminated with anabolic steroids [4]. A 2015 Consumer Reports test reported unsafe levels of arsenic, cadmium, lead and mercury in several protein powders, and a 2015 CBC investigation alleged protein spiking with amino-acid filler, which many companies disputed [6]. Grokipedia notes that few high-calorie products have batch-level third-party testing for banned substances, which matters to athletes under anti-doping rules [1].

Common complaints include bloating, gas and cramping, particularly with lactose-containing whey; Grokipedia also lists unwanted fat gain from surplus calories and nutrient imbalance if shakes replace whole foods [1]. A 2025 case report in the Pakistan Journal of Medical Sciences describes life-threatening pancreatitis with panniculitis associated with a weight-gain supplement; the report notes that mass gainers containing anabolic steroids have been linked in the literature to acute pancreatitis [5].

In looksmaxxing, mass gainers are tied to the goal of adding mass for a larger frame and fuller physique. Looksmax.org threads discuss them under bulking and supplements, with some users reporting that they stopped using mass gainers, protein powder and creatine and others defending them [2]. The debate commonly turns on whole food versus powder, digestive comfort and skin, with at least one user suspecting that the products contributed to acne and gut problems [2].

No clinical trials of mass gainer powders as a product have been found. A registered trial of overfeeding combined with resistance training in 32 participants (started 2019) examined body composition changes under a calorie surplus, and is about overfeeding generally rather than a commercial gainer [3]. Grokipedia cites a 2002 randomized trial of high-calorie supplements with resistance training that reported gains in body mass and fat-free mass, and notes that many trials are small, short and sometimes industry-funded [1]. Related research on protein supplementation, summarised in the 2018 meta-analysis, reports gains in strength and muscle size, with diminishing returns above about 1.6 g per kg per day [1][6].

timeline.event: Eugen Sandow promotes dietary control for muscle growth [6].
Irvin P. Johnson popularises egg-based protein powders among bodybuilders [6].
New Zealand's dairy industry produces a drink-soluble whey protein concentrate, developed after a request from Coca-Cola [7].
Bodybuilders promote homemade high-calorie shakes; commercial weight-gain powders follow [1][6].
DSHEA signed into law on 25 October, placing dietary supplements under food-style regulation [4][9].
Consumer Reports reports heavy metals in several protein powders, and a CBC investigation alleges protein spiking [6].
Meta-analysis finds protein supplementation enhances strength and muscle gains in resistance training [6].
A trial of overfeeding plus resistance training begins, registered as NCT04069351 [3].
Case report links a weight-gain supplement to pancreatitis with panniculitis [5].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, mass gainers come up in discussions of bulking and supplements, with users split on whether they are useful [2].

claims.claim: Mass gainers harm gut health and may cause acne, so whole food is better.
claims.believers: One looksmax.org user who stopped using mass gainers, protein powder and creatine said he suspected the ingredients were poorly absorbed, disrupted his gut and may have contributed to his acne [2].
claims.experts: No published study cited here has tested mass gainer powders for acne or gut effects; the available documented harms involve adulterated products [4][5].

claims.claim: Carbs and calories matter more than large amounts of protein for gaining.
claims.believers: Some forum replies argue that a moderate protein intake is enough and extra calories should come from carbohydrate, while others in the thread disagreed strongly [2].
claims.experts: Recommended protein intakes differ (0.8 g/kg/day RDA versus about 1.2 to 1.8 g/kg/day suggested for athletes), and reviews disagree about benefits of high protein intake [4].

claims.claim: Mass gainers are the fastest way for a hardgainer to add size.
claims.believers: Lifters who struggle to eat enough say a liquid-calorie shake is easier than extra meals, and describe using them while bulking [1][2].
claims.experts: Sources describe weight gain as depending on a calorie surplus together with resistance training; no trials have compared mass gainers with equivalent whole-food calories [1][3].

claims.claim: Plain protein plus whole food does the same job more cleanly.
claims.believers: Other forum members prefer whole food or plain protein [2].
claims.experts: Maltodextrin is a fast-digesting carbohydrate with a high glycemic index [8]; Wikipedia states that people with a balanced diet do not need protein supplements [10].

claims.claim: Supplements labelled as mass gainers are safe because they are sold over the counter.
claims.believers: Supplement labels list ingredients and amounts.
claims.experts: Under DSHEA manufacturers confirm their own product safety, and studies have found undeclared steroids in some muscle-building products [4][9].
